newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N.'s Iraq monitoring criticized by U.S., Britain.
newsitem.headline: U.N.'s Iraq monitoring criticized by U.S., Britain.

text.p: U.S. and British officials said on Wednesday the United Nations needed to step up its monitoring of the distribution of goods in Iraq under the "oil-for-food" deal.
"We are not entirely satisfied with the implementation so far by the Iraqis and by the (U.N.) secretariat," U.S. ambassador Bill Richardson told reporters.
Said British ambassador Sir John Weston: "One of the points to which we attach importance is that there should be proper monitoring in the way these humanitarian supplies are distributed."

Richardson spoke after the Security Council approved a six-month renewal of the plan under which Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other necessities to help alleviate the effects of sanctions imposed after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

"They (the U.N.) need to provide better and more timely and accurate information, specifically on Iraq's distribution methods, the operation in the north, and other implementation facets that are not being properly handled," he said.
He was referring to measures, including on-the-spot U.N. monitoring, to ensure the fair distribution of humanitarian supplies among all sectors of the Iraqi population.
In the largely Kurdish-inhabited north of Iraq, the United Nations is in charge of distribution. In the rest of the country, Iraqi authorities are responsible subject to U.N. monitoring.
Richardson added: "We don't have sufficient data. We think that the secretariat needs to provide more accurate data there. We think the Iraqis have been playing games with statistics, with figures."
Richardson said these issues would be "crucial in future decisions" regarding the "oil-for-food" deal.
Asked about any increase in the $2 billion worth of oil sales permitted, he replied: "We don't think that's needed. We don't think an increase in oil sales is needed."

Another U.S. official said that in one case, an Iraqi minister summoned U.N. observers to his office and told them what they could and could not do, but the United Nations did not report this incident or similar ones.

He said the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs, which is in charge of the monitoring, was not equipped to do the job. The agency was geared towards helping disaster victims or refugees and was used to cooperating with local authorities rather than confronting them.
Under-Secretary General Yasushi Akashi, head of the department, told reporters after briefing the council that it saw no need to increase the size of Iraqi oil sales.

"I think by and large, council members are satisfied, fully satisfied, with the way we are doing our distribution work, as well as our observation work," Akashi said. He conceded that "one delegation (said) they would have liked to have somewhat greater detail."
"If there is any additional need for transparency we will certainly reflect it in our future reports," Akashi said.
